name: Therapy / counselling

lead: Therapy or counselling means working with a trained professional through structured conversation to change thoughts, behaviour or emotional patterns. In looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion it is mentioned as a way to support self-esteem alongside, or instead of, appearance changes.
General psychotherapy has an extensive research base across many conditions. Studies aimed specifically at appearance-related self-esteem in the looksmaxxing context were not found.

paras: Approaches include cognitive-behavioural, humanistic, psychodynamic, systemic and expressive therapies. Many researchers attribute part of the benefit to common factors such as the therapeutic relationship.[1]
Reported limitations include high dropout (roughly 30 to 60 percent), unclear mechanisms of change and uneven outcomes between individuals.[1] Cost and access vary by country.

lead: Therapy or counselling, formally psychotherapy, is the use of psychological methods, usually through regular personal interaction with a trained practitioner, to help people change behaviour, improve well-being and work through problems.[1] It is listed on the wiki as a lifestyle meta because it is sometimes raised as a form of support for self-esteem.

Many schools exist, including cognitive-behavioural, humanistic, psychodynamic, systemic and expressive therapies, and many practitioners blend them.[1] A 2022 umbrella review summarised on Wikipedia found generally small effect sizes for psychotherapy across conditions, and different methods often produce similar outcomes.[1]
No published trial found in the research reviewed here tests therapy as a looksmaxxing intervention or for appearance-specific self-esteem outcomes.

paras: Psychotherapy is described by the American Psychological Association as the informed and intentional application of clinical methods and interpersonal stances to help people change.[1] Cognitive-behavioural approaches, which emerged in the 1960s and 1970s, and humanistic approaches that emphasise personal growth are among the families most often linked to self-esteem work.[1]

Wikipedia summarises that psychotherapy shows general efficacy across many conditions, that outcomes vary by person, and that shared factors such as the therapeutic relationship may matter greatly.[1] Critics cited there raise concerns about unclear mechanisms of change, possible adverse effects, cultural assumptions and dropout rates between about 30 and 60 percent.[1]

No studies found for therapy as a looksmaxxing practice or for appearance-specific self-esteem. Randomised trials of psychological interventions exist for other populations, for example glycaemic control in diabetes,[2][3] depression and anxiety in dementia,[4] and depression in dialysis patients,[5] but these address different conditions and outcomes.
